questions.q: About how many objects are tracked circling Earth, and how many of them are working satellites?
questions.do: Read the introduction at the top of the page. You can also check the last points on the Counting the junk chart.
questions.a: About 40,000 tracked objects (40,230 in 2025), but only about 11,000 working satellites. The rest is junk: dead satellites, spent rocket stages and fragments.

questions.q: Compare the two real breakups. How long until half the fragments have fallen back?
questions.do: In Break something, click Mission Shakti, 2019 and read Half have fallen by. Then click Iridium–Kosmos, 2009 and read it again.
questions.a: Mission Shakti (283 km): about 5 days. Iridium–Kosmos (789 km): about 59 years. The page calls the first “Self-cleaning” and the second “Here to stay”.

questions.q: Start from Mission Shakti and raise only the height to 500 km. What happens to the debris?
questions.do: Click Mission Shakti, 2019. Move Height of the breakup to 500 km, keep the other sliders the same, and click Break it and watch.
questions.a: Half have fallen only after about 14 months (instead of 5 days), and the last piece takes about 78 years. A little more height buys a lot more time, because the air thins out so quickly with height.

questions.q: The model says the last Mission Shakti piece falls after 17 months. The real last piece re-entered in 2022, about three years later. Why the difference?
questions.do: Read the second row of the Checks table, and the note in What the model leaves out.
questions.a: 2019–2020 was a quiet-Sun minimum. When the Sun is quiet, the upper air is thinner than this model’s average, so there is less drag and the real pieces stayed up longer.

questions.q: What happened in space in 2009 at 789 km, and how much debris did it leave?
questions.do: Read the introduction, click Iridium–Kosmos, 2009, and read the footer’s source notes and the third row of Checks.
questions.a: Two satellites, Iridium 33 and Kosmos 2251, collided at 789 km at 11.7 km/s. Over 2,000 fragments were catalogued by July 2011. At that height the air is too thin to clear them quickly.
